transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-03
Time: 15:00 PDT (UTC-7)
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jodie Park (Redwood SRE); Priya Rao (Nimbus Head of Platform), Marcus Li (Nimbus Infra), Olga Petrov (Nimbus Security), Diego Ramos (Nimbus Product)
External links referenced: playbook draft (https://redwood.run/playbooks/regional-fallback), benchmark sheet (https://sheets.example.com/nimbus-kv-warmstart)

[00:00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we wanted to run through the delegated failover pattern and how KV warmstart can help avoid tail latency during region cutovers. Quick intro?
[00:00:12] Priya: Hi, Priya here. We're responsible for platform reliability at Nimbus. Marcus will run the tests and Olga's on security and compliance.
[00:00:20] Marcus: Hey.
[00:00:22] Alex: Samir, want to kick off with the high-level plan?
[00:00:25] Samir: Sure. So there are three parts: routing policy, capacity footprint per region, and cache warmstart. Routing — we propose delegated routing where edge proxies use policy to route to regional clusters and fall back to remote regions only after local capacity is saturated or latency SLOs breach. That minimizes cross-region egress and cost.
[00:00:44] Marcus: When you say "delegated" do you mean the edge decides or a control-plane decision?
[00:00:48] Samir: Edge decides with a small control-plane sync. Edge has a live policy with thresholds: in-flight requests, queue depth, p99 latency. If thresholds hit, it flips a local flag and routes to a pre-configured fallback region.
[00:01:03] Diego: Is that sticky? Will ongoing chats move regions mid-session?
[00:01:08] Jodie: We recommend sticky sessions for stateful KV-backed chat. The plan is session stickiness with a session affinity TTL. If you evacuate a region, we run a transfer with KV warmstart so new tokens bring the cache with them — avoids cold-start decoding penalties.
[00:01:28] Olga: Quick security note: cross-region copy of KV might interact with your KMS policies and data residency. We need exact KMS key ARNs and whether keys are multi-region.
[00:01:39] Alex: Good call. We'll add that to the action items.
[00:01:45] Priya: On capacity, what's the recommended headroom? We saw the doc that suggested 25% but our traffic shape is spiky — weekend batch jobs plus spikes.
[00:01:57] Samir: For spiky workloads we typically recommend 40% headroom cap on model instances per region, and a warmpool for 5–10% of peak reserved as burst. That allows routing to keep requests local while providing capacity for sudden spikes. The warmpool can be burstable and billed differently on Dedicated.
[00:02:18] Marcus: Are these warm pools GPU warm or just container warm?
[00:02:22] Samir: GPU warm — kernel and model loaded; KV warmstart is separate.
[00:02:25] Marcus: Understood.
[00:02:28] [00:02:30] Alex: Let's talk KV warmstart. Samir?
[00:02:31] Samir: KV warmstart is pre-populating model KV cache with likely prefixes so first token latency drops dramatically. We support snapshotting the KV cache and streaming it to a target region in advance. Two modes: eager pre-warm (bulk snapshot transfer at low traffic hours) or progressive warm (on-demand prime for top N sessions).
[00:02:54] Priya: How big are these snapshots typically? We run a lot of multimodal contexts.
[00:03:00] Samir: Depends. For textual sessions they're small per session, but aggregate can be multiple GBs. For long context on multimodal you might need tens of GB. Compression and delta encoding help — we only transfer active entries.
[00:03:13] Marcus: Any risk of inconsistency? If a session updates earlier state and we shipped a stale KV snapshot?
[00:03:20] Samir: We ensure strong consistency by applying a version vector and a short quiesce period: during snapshot we halt writes to session shard for a second or two, then resume. We'll document the window — typical window is <5s but depends on traffic.
[00:03:34] Diego: That could be tricky for financial workflows.
[00:03:37] Olga: Exactly — need audit log line items for snapshot creation and transfer. Also SAML/SSO to the control plane for access.
[00:03:44] Jodie: We'll add audit hooks; Redwood's private install supports forwarding syslog and long-term audit retention.
[00:03:49] [00:04:00] Alex: There's an operational playbook we suggested — stepwise failover: 1) failover readiness check, 2) pre-warm KV snapshots to target region, 3) flip routing flags, 4) monitor tail latency and revert if needed.
[00:04:14] Marcus: During stage 2 how long does warmstart take?
[00:04:18] Samir: For a shard with 10k active sessions we saw ~8–12 minutes for progressive warm, less for eager if network is good. If you're doing greedy bulk transfer of everything it can be longer.
[00:04:29] Priya: So we should schedule this during low traffic windows.
[00:04:33] Samir: Exactly. We recommended 02:00–04:00 UTC for Nimbus given your traffic.
[00:04:38] Diego: What about quantization? We want to push cost down, but worried about quality regresses.
[00:04:44] Samir: Quantization reduces memory and improves throughput but affects sampling tail characteristics slightly. For latency SLOs we recommend dynamic quantization on transformer weights and per-layer calibration. We can run shadow comparisons against your eval prompts in Redwood Optimize.
[00:04:59] Priya: Can the quantized models live in a fallback region only?
[00:05:03] Samir: Yes — routing policies can prefer non-quantized in primary region and quantized variants in fallback; we call that "tiered-model routing." If fallback is engaged we route to cheaper quantized profile to save cost.
[00:05:13] Marcus: Any observable jitter when switching models mid-session?
[00:05:17] Jodie: If you switch model variant mid-session you risk output drift. We recommend model-boundary at session restart or graceful degrade with a version mapping. During live evacuation we prefer to maintain the same model family; only swap to quantized if there's severe capacity pressure and after a canary.
[00:05:35] Olga: From security standpoint, quantized model artifacts stored in other regions must still be encrypted with your KMS — not Redwood's default.
[00:05:42] Alex: We'll capture those KMS requirements.
[00:05:47] [00:06:00] Marcus: On networking, can the control-plane initiate the warmstart transfer or does customer need to push?
[00:06:06] Samir: Both. For Private deployments, customers can opt-in to let Redwood trigger snapshot exports and peer to target VPC via a peering/tunnel. For fully air-gapped installs, customer must run internal transfer jobs; Redwood provides tooling.
[00:06:19] Priya: We are in a hybrid mode — private control plane but VPC peering allowed.
[00:06:24] Samir: Good; that means we can automate the snapshot push. We'll need IAM roles and temporary credentials.
[00:06:30] Olga: Also please make sure tokens are non-exportable in logs. We can't have secrets in transit in plaintext.
[00:06:36] Jodie: Our transfer uses envelope encryption — payloads encrypted with customer KMS keys before egress.
[00:06:42] [00:07:00] Diego: For the actual failover test, can we do a partial regional evacuation to validate logs and metrics?
[00:07:05] Alex: Yes — we propose three stages: canary (2% traffic to fallback + KV warm), partial (20%), full (100%). Each stage waits for p95/p99 signal windows.
[00:07:18] Marcus: What's the rollback time target?
[00:07:21] Samir: We aim for sub-5 minute rollback to previous routing state if SLOs breach. The control-plane keeps snapshots of last-good config to flip back quickly.
[00:07:31] Priya: Is there an automated rollback or manual?
[00:07:34] Samir: Both. Auto-rollback is enabled by default with thresholds you can tune; we usually have manual gates for production.
[00:07:40] [00:08:00] Olga: For compliance, we need a playbook step that enumerates all artifacts created during failover with timestamps for audit.
[00:08:07] Jodie: We'll add an action item to produce the audit artifact template.
[00:08:11] Alex: Let's demo a sample metric flow — Samir, can you explain how we detect a region is degraded?
[00:08:16] Samir: We use a combination: queue depth over threshold, p99 > SLO for 3 consecutive windows, and error budget burn. The edge also calculates a weighted score across these signals.
[00:08:28] Marcus: Does that include GPU saturation and kernel stalls?
[00:08:31] Samir: Yes, we ingest GPU telemetry (SM utilization, memory pressure, microstalls) if agent is allowed in the private cluster. If not, we rely on host-level metrics.
[00:08:40] [00:09:00] Diego: Any pitfalls to watch for when the fallback region has different model variants or quantization?
[00:09:06] Samir: Main risks are behavioral drift and token alignment differences. To mitigate, we pin model family and tokenizer, and run A/B of responses in canary. Also we ensure sampling seed continuity where possible.
[00:09:20] Priya: Can we get a list of recommended regression eval prompts to monitor?
[00:09:24] Samir: We'll produce a tailored eval set based on your top N prompts — action item for Samir.
[00:09:28] [00:10:00] Alex: A few real-world notes: we saw a customer who did an eager bulk KV warm and still had a small p99 blip because their session affinity TTL was short. So TTL tuning matters.
[00:10:13] Marcus: What's a good TTL?
[00:10:15] Samir: Depends. For chat 30–60s affinity often works; for longer sessions you may keep affinity tied to session lifecycle.
[00:10:23] Olga: Also consider retention rules for PII inside KV. We need a mapping of what gets serialized to KV.
[00:10:29] Jodie: Redwood provides a sanitizer hook and a denylist for keys. We'll share the config example.
[00:10:36] [00:11:00] Priya: Can we talk about cost? Cross-region egress plus storing extra quantized artifacts — how to estimate?
[00:11:08] Alex: We'll send a cost model. Roughly: egress per GB + storage for KV snapshots + extra reserved capacity. Using tiered-model routing you only pay for quantized serving when fallback is used. We'll run a spreadsheet with your request mix.
[00:11:25] Diego: Could autoscaling cause flapping during failover?
[00:11:28] Samir: It can. That's why we use cooldown windows and temporary "evacuation mode" that pauses aggressive downscaling until traffic stabilizes.
[00:11:37] Marcus: Any recommended observability dashboards?
[00:11:40] Jodie: Per-route p95/p99, queue depth, KV hit rate, kernel stalls, and a routing-score panel. We'll share a Grafana bundle.
[00:11:49] [00:12:30] Alex: Quick interlude — some transcription note: the auto transcript sometimes writes "K V cache" as separate; ignore those minor typos in the doc.
[00:12:40] Priya: Thanks.
[00:12:44] [00:13:00] Priya: One more question — are there API hooks for us to tag sessions as "critical" so routing prefers local region?
[00:13:05] Samir: Yes, we provide session priority tags and routing can be policy-aware, giving priority to critical sessions. That would bypass fallback unless forced.
[00:13:15] Diego: That sounds useful for payment flows.
[00:13:18] Olga: On the legal side, we need to mark which sessions can cross borders. We'll provide a compliance matrix.
[00:13:24] Alex: We'll make sure playbook includes jurisdiction gates.
[00:13:29] [00:14:00] Marcus: For the bench test, what metrics should we collect?
[00:14:04] Samir: Collect p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput, KV hit/miss ratio, cold-start frequent token latency, GPU util, error rate, and end-to-end user-perceived latency. Also trace ids to correlate.
[00:14:17] Priya: We'll add those to the sheet.
[00:14:22] [00:15:00] Alex: Ok let's move to a scenario walk-through — staging canary with KV progressive warm: step 0 prepare snapshot list, step 1 push top-100 session keys to eu-west-1, step 2 route 2% to fallback, step 3 measure for 30 minutes, step 4 expand to 20% if stable.
[00:15:37] Diego: Who owns step 1?
[00:15:39] Samir: Samir and Marcus jointly — Samir will run the Redwood tooling, Marcus will approve pushes in your VPC.
[00:15:46] [00:16:00] Marcus: Any expected tooling errors?
[00:16:03] Samir: We sometimes see transient timeouts; the tooling retries idempotently. We'll surface errors and keep a retry log.
[00:16:10] Olga: Will this require opening inbound ports? We are strict on ingress.
[00:16:14] Samir: No inbound — we use egress from your VPC to push into a pre-signed bucket in the target region.
[00:16:20] Jodie: And payloads are encrypted client-side.
[00:16:23] [00:17:00] Diego: If the fallback region lacks GPU capacity, do you fall back to CPU or queued responses?
[00:17:09] Samir: We can route to lower-tier CPU endpoints as a last resort, but latency will be much higher. We prefer to have some reserved GPU capacity in each fallback region.
[00:17:19] Priya: Ok that confirms our need for a small reserved pool in each AZ.
[00:17:23] [00:18:00] Alex: Any questions about the control-plane interface?
[00:18:03] Marcus: Is there a way to preview the routing decision tree?
[00:18:07] Samir: Yes, the console has a "routing simulator" where you can inject metrics and see decisions. We'll give access in a read-only role.
[00:18:16] Diego: Nice.
[00:18:20] [00:19:00] Olga: From compliance — can we get signed SOC2 artifacts?
[00:19:04] Alex: Yes, we'll share the SOC two pack and the private deployment whitepaper.
[00:19:09] Olga: Also we need a list of subprocessors.
[00:19:12] Alex: We'll include that.
[00:19:16] [00:20:00] Samir: Quick note on batching: batching increases throughput but can increase tail latency if you wait to fill a batch. For interactive SLOs we recommend short max batch window (2–8 ms) and adaptive batching — batch only when in-flight requests are high.
[00:20:31] Marcus: Does batching interact with KV warmstart?
[00:20:34] Samir: Yes — if KV is cold, the first few batches see higher latency; warmstart reduces that. Also batching can reduce effective p99 because more tokens amortized.
[00:20:44] [00:21:00] Priya: Are there observability hooks in our private console for KV snapshot transfers?
[00:21:04] Jodie: Yes — transfer progress, checksums, and transfer RTT are exposed.
[00:21:09] Diego: Great.
[00:21:15] [00:22:00] Alex: Time check — about 50 minutes left. Any major concerns we haven't covered?
[00:22:09] Olga: Data residency and KMS integration — need concrete artifact list.
[00:22:13] Alex: Action item captured.
[00:22:18] Priya: We also want a dry-run of canary with synthetic traffic first.
[00:22:22] Samir: Agreed; synthetic traffic reduces blast radius for initial tests.
[00:22:27] [00:23:00] Diego: Can the routing policy be exported as IaC?
[00:23:03] Samir: Yes, policies are expressed as YAML and can be managed through Terraform or Redwood CLI. We'll share a sample repo.
[00:23:11] Marcus: Nice.
[00:23:16] [00:24:00] Alex: Let's capture the rough timeline agreed: by 2026-03-05 Redwood sends cost delta & playbook; Nimbus confirms test window by 2026-03-08; warmstart benchmark runs 2026-03-09; follow-up sync after results 2026-03-12.
[00:24:30] Priya: That works.
[00:24:34] [00:25:00] Alex: Any last technical clarifications?
[00:25:03] Marcus: For KVS sharding — do you recommend session-based or user-based sharding?
[00:25:09] Samir: Session-based yields easier locality for chat; user-based helps multi-device continuity. Depends on your product; we can prototype both.
[00:25:18] Diego: We'll start with session-based.
[00:25:21] [00:26:00] Olga: Also, please confirm deletion workflows — when a session is deleted, how quickly do you purge KV across regions?
[00:26:29] Jodie: Deletion is propagated via event stream and we ensure TTL+immediate purge for PII flagged keys. We'll share SLAs.
[00:26:40] [00:27:00] Alex: Ok wrapping up — recap of next steps and owners. Samir will run bench and share tailored eval set; Alex will send pricing; Jodie will share audit template; Priya & Marcus to confirm test window and CIDRs; Olga to send KMS ARNs and subprocessor questions.
[00:27:25] Priya: Confirmed.
[00:27:29] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by email and post the playbook link.
[00:27:35] Marcus: Thanks.
[00:27:38] Diego: Appreciate it.
[00:27:40] Olga: Bye.
